C1.heading: Develop your user and customer discovery skills
C1.concept: Product discovery is how product teams understand customers' problems, check whether a problem is worth solving and explore possible solutions before committing to build one.
subtopics: Identifying the user's problem, not just the requested feature
Interviewing users about specific past experiences
Synthesising notes into a few clear findings
Testing the riskiest assumption before building
C1.why: Product Managers are expected to bring evidence about users into decisions. Showing that you can learn from users, and change a decision because of it, is one of the clearest signals of product thinking.
C1.why_bridge: In an Associate Product Manager role you would usually support discovery on features; arriving with interview and synthesis practice lets you take on more of it.

learn.summary: Start with the free GOV.UK guides on discovery research and interviews, then watch 'How to Talk to Users'.
Read The Mom Test before your first interviews; read Continuous Discovery Habits once you have done a few.
If you prefer a structured course, the University of Virginia's fundamentals course covers customer discovery alongside other product methods.

engineering: Pick a feature or workflow your team is building or has just shipped.
Ask the product owner or manager whether you can join, or run, three to five short conversations with its users or with the internal teams who support them.
Ask about the last time each person did the task: what happened, what was hard, what they did instead. Avoid asking whether they would like your idea.
Write up what you heard and propose one change, then ask to be part of the decision about it.
analysis: Choose a process or report your stakeholders rely on.
Run three to five short conversations about how they actually use it and where it fails them, using specific recent examples.
Combine what you heard with the usage data you can already see.
Write the problem statement and recommend one change to whoever decides.
customer: Choose a recurring customer problem you hear about.
Review recent tickets or calls and speak with three to five customers about specific instances.
Separate the underlying problem from the solutions customers suggest.
Write a problem statement and share it with the product team.
default: Choose a product you use, or a service at your organisation, with a clear group of users.
Speak with three to five of its users about the last time they used it, using a short discussion guide.
Synthesise the conversations into a few findings.
Write a problem statement and one proposed change. If this is a personal project, label it as one.

output.name: Discovery summary
good_contains: Who you spoke with and why
Three to five findings, each backed by what people said or did
A one-sentence problem statement
The change you propose and the riskiest assumption behind it
What happened next, if the work was real

use_output: As a concrete example of learning from users in interviews
As the basis of a case study
As evidence for a conversation about taking on product work
Added to your Trace profile once it reflects real work

C2.heading: Develop product direction and roadmap thinking
C2.concept: Product strategy is a clear choice about which problems a product will solve, for whom and why now. A roadmap turns that direction into a sequenced, regularly revised plan of outcomes, not a fixed list of features.
subtopics: Writing a short product direction: problem, audience and goal
Revisiting priorities with data and research
C2.why: Setting and explaining direction is one of the decisions that separates product ownership from delivery or analysis. Employers look for evidence that you have shaped what gets built and why.
C2.why_bridge: An Associate Product Manager usually contributes to a roadmap rather than owning a product's strategy, so you will need to seek opportunities to shape direction for a feature area.

learn.summary: Read the free GOV.UK guides on developing a roadmap and deciding on priorities.
INSPIRED explains how product vision and strategy work in technology companies.
The University of Virginia course covers building an actionable, testable focus for a product.

engineering: Pick an area you know well, such as an internal tool, a platform component or a feature set.
Write a one-page direction: the problem, who it is for, the outcome you want and what you would not do.
Draft a next-quarter roadmap of three to five outcomes in priority order, with your reasoning.
Review it with whoever owns the area and ask what they would change and why.
analysis: Pick a product area your analysis supports.
Write a one-page direction backed by the data you already have.
Turn it into a sequenced roadmap of outcomes, not features.
Present it to the area's owner and record the decisions it informed.
customer: Pick a customer segment you know well.
Write the direction you would set for them, based on the problems you see most.
Share it with the product team as a proposal.
default: Pick a product you know well.
Write a one-page direction and a roadmap of three to five outcomes in priority order.
Explain what you chose not to do.
If this is a personal project, label it clearly as one.

output.name: Product direction and roadmap
good_contains: The problem and who it is for
The outcome you are aiming at and how you would know
Three to five sequenced outcomes with the reason for the order
What you are deliberately not doing
Feedback from the area's owner, if it was real work

use_output: To discuss product thinking in interviews
As a proposal to take on roadmap work in your current role
As part of a case study

C3.heading: Turn problems into clear requirements and priorities
C3.concept: Requirements describe what a product needs to do and why, from the user's point of view, with criteria that tell the team when it is done. Prioritising them means deciding what comes first and explaining the trade-off.
subtopics: User stories: who, what and why
C3.why: Product Managers are expected to turn a problem into something a team can build, and to decide its order. It is often the first responsibility people take on when moving into product work.
C3.why_bridge: Associate Product Managers often own requirements for a feature, so this is a natural first area of ownership in a bridge role.

learn.summary: Read the free GOV.UK guides on writing user stories and deciding on priorities.

engineering: Take one real piece of work your team is about to start.
Write the user stories and acceptance criteria before work begins, and agree the priority order with the team.
Follow it through to delivery and note what changed and why.
analysis: Take a request you are working on.
Rewrite it as user stories with acceptance criteria and a proposed priority.
Agree it with the team that will build it.
customer: Take a customer request that keeps coming back.
Write it up as a user story with acceptance criteria and evidence of the need.
Share it with the product team as a proposal.
default: Take a feature of a product you know.
Write user stories, acceptance criteria and a priority order with your reasons.
If this is a personal project, label it as one.

output.name: Prioritised requirements
good_contains: User stories with acceptance criteria
The priority order and why
What was delivered and what changed along the way, if it was real work

use_output: As evidence of turning a problem into buildable work

C4.heading: Learn to define outcome metrics and decide from data
C4.concept: An outcome metric shows whether a change actually helped users or the business, rather than whether work was delivered. Product Managers define it before building, then use the result to decide what to do next.
subtopics: Turning a goal into a testable hypothesis
Choosing a small set of metrics and a baseline
Making and recording the follow-up decision
C4.why: Owning the measure of success, and acting on it, is one of the clearest signs of product ownership. Analysing or reporting numbers is useful, but it is different from defining the outcome and deciding from it.
C4.why_bridge: In an Associate Product Manager role you may recommend decisions from data; seek a feature where you define the success metric yourself and make the follow-up decision.

learn.summary: Read the free GOV.UK guide on setting performance metrics, then take the free Udacity A/B Testing course.
Lean Analytics helps you choose the one metric that matters; Trustworthy Online Controlled Experiments is the reference for later, once you run experiments.

engineering: Pick a feature or change your team is about to ship.
Before it ships, agree with the product owner what outcome it should change, which metric shows it and the current baseline.
Write up what it showed and what was decided next, and ask to make or recommend that decision.
analysis: Pick a change your stakeholders are about to make.
Propose the outcome metric and baseline before it happens, not only a report afterwards.
After the change, recommend the decision and record what was decided.
Note whether you defined the metric and made the decision, or supported someone else's: be precise about which.
customer: Pick a change that affects your customers.
Agree how its success will be measured before it happens.
Review the result and recommend a next step.
default: Pick a feature of a product you know.
Write its outcome metric, baseline and decision rule.
If you can observe real data, check it afterwards; otherwise label this as a learning exercise.

output.name: Metric definition and decision record
good_contains: The outcome you wanted and why
The metric, how it is measured and the baseline
The decision rule you agreed in advance
What happened and the decision made
Your exact role in it

use_output: As the strongest single example of product ownership you can show
For analytical and metrics interview questions

C5.heading: Build cross-functional collaboration without authority
C5.concept: Product Managers align engineering, design, business and leadership around decisions they don't control directly. That means preparing options, running the discussion and making the decision and its reasons visible.
C5.why: Most product work happens through other people. Showing that you can get several functions to a decision is a core part of the role.
C5.why_bridge: A bridge role puts you in these conversations daily; aim to lead some of them rather than only attend.

default: Find a decision that involves at least two other functions.
Prepare the options and trade-offs, run the discussion and circulate the decision and its reasons.
Ask one participant for feedback on how it went.

output.name: Decision record
good_contains: The options considered
The decision and who agreed
The reasons and trade-offs

use_output: For behavioural interview questions about influence
As part of a case study

C6.heading: Show iterative delivery across the lifecycle
C6.concept: Iterative delivery means shipping in small steps, measuring what happened and adjusting, from first release to retirement.
subtopics: Deciding to iterate, expand or stop
C6.why: Product Managers are expected to keep improving a product after launch, not only to get it shipped.
C6.why_bridge: Bridge roles usually involve regular releases; use them to practise measuring and iterating.

default: Pick something your team shipped recently.
Look at what happened after release and propose one iteration.
Follow it through and record the decision.

output.name: Iteration note
good_contains: What shipped
What you observed afterwards
The iteration and why

use_output: To discuss delivery and iteration in interviews

alternatives.workplace: Ask to take on this responsibility for a feature or workflow in your current job. Usually the most valuable evidence, because it is real work.
alternatives.internal: Shadow or work alongside a Product Manager in your organisation on one decision or release.
alternatives.mentorship: Ask an experienced Product Manager to review your output and talk through how they would approach it.
alternatives.personal_project: Do the exercise on a product you know. Label it clearly as a personal project: it shows how you think, not professional ownership.
alternatives.internship: An internship or returnship can give supervised product experience. It is usually most suitable earlier in a career or after a break.

themes.title: Technical delivery and execution
themes.relevance: This gives you a useful foundation for working closely with engineering teams on how and when product work gets built and shipped.

themes.title: Working with cross-functional teams
themes.relevance: Product Managers spend much of their time aligning people they don't manage, so this is directly useful.

themes.title: Understanding customers and users
themes.relevance: Understanding what users need is central to product work, and this experience gives you a starting point.

themes.title: Shaping requirements and priorities
themes.relevance: Turning needs into clear, prioritised work is one of the first responsibilities people take on in product roles.

themes.title: Working with data
themes.relevance: Comfort with data helps you define and read the measures product decisions depend on.

themes.title: Product direction and outcomes
themes.relevance: This is close to the core of the Product Manager role: setting direction and being accountable for results.

area_phrases.delivery_execution: delivering and releasing work with your team

resume: Lead with the experience that is closest to product work, described in plain language.
Describe your role precisely: what you did, what you decided and what you supported.
Add new product work only once it is real, and say what it was.
case_study: Context: the product, the users and the situation
The problem and how you knew it mattered
Your role: exactly what you were responsible for
What you did and the options you considered
What happened, only if you know
What you learned and would do differently
narratives: Prepare two or three short stories from real work, each with the situation, your action and the result.
Have one story about learning from users, one about a trade-off you made and one about working across teams.
never_claim: Metrics or results you can't support
A personal project presented as professional work

interviews: Product sense: improve or design a product for a given user and problem
Analytical: choose metrics, diagnose a drop, size a market
Execution: prioritise, plan a launch, handle a trade-off
Behavioural: influence, conflict, failure and learning
Technical (often asked of engineers moving into product): explain a system and its trade-offs simply
product_case: Pick a product you use. In 45 minutes, write who it is for, the most important problem, three solution options, the one you'd choose, the metric you'd track and the main trade-off.
Repeat with different products until the structure feels natural; ask a practitioner to review one.
networking: Speak with two or three people already doing the target role about how they got in and what their teams look for.
Ask for a referral only where someone knows your work.
internal: Ask your manager or product team whether product roles or projects are open to internal candidates and what they would want to see.

weekly_advice.1_3: With about 1–3 hours a week, work on one development area at a time. Start with the free resource and one small practical exercise before adding anything else.
weekly_advice.4_6: With about 4–6 hours a week, combine one learning resource with one practical opportunity at a time.
weekly_advice.7_10: With about 7–10 hours a week, you can work on a learning resource and a practical exercise in parallel, and start interview practice earlier.
weekly_advice.more_than_10: With more than 10 hours a week, you can work on two development areas in parallel while building your case study.
weekly_advice.varies: Because your time varies, keep one small practical exercise going and pick up learning when you have time.
